narrative:
The model determined that you have a 52% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tips just above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction toward failure. Placing in the second decile is noticeably lower than the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted, signaling weaker performance in later law-school years. This was the main reason the model leaned toward predicting you would struggle with the bar.

Your LSAT score worked in the opposite direction and was the second-most important factor. At 35.5, it sits slightly below the 37.2 average of accepted students, yet the model still viewed it as a modest positive signal that pulled the prediction back toward passing.

Your first-year class ranking came third. Finishing in the bottom decile, compared with an average around the sixth decile for accepted applicants, added another clear push toward predicting failure.

Taken together, the two low class rankings outweighed the decent LSAT and produced a failure probability just high enough to trigger rejection.

What you should do next is straightforward: retake key courses to raise your upper-year grades, then retake the LSAT aiming for at least a 38. Stronger numbers in those two areas would likely flip the prediction and open the door to admission.
